Este bloque trata de lo que se puede con: This block is about what can be counted and computed with discrete objects: points and lines, sequences, steps of an algorithm, bits, moves. The tools are the usual ones, counting as in [[pe-combinatoria|combinatorics]], adding and taking logarithms, and the idea from [[av-topologia|topology]] that the exact shape does not matter, only the connections. We start with the simplest object of all.
Un <strong>grafo</strong> es lo más simp: A graph is the simplest thing imaginable: some points (vertices) and some lines joining them (edges). Nothing more. And with that you model social networks, the underground, the internet, delivery routes, molecules, a school timetable and the road map of a country.
Lo único que importa es <strong>quién es: The only thing that matters is who is connected to whom. Where you draw the points or whether the lines are straight or curved makes no difference at all: it is pure topology.
Que cosas tan distintas como una red de: For things as different as an underground network, the friendships of a social network or the tasks of a building site with their dependencies to be studied with the same tools, half a dozen words are needed first.

<strong>Camino</strong>: sucesión de ari: Path: a succession of edges leading from one vertex to another.
<strong>Ciclo</strong>: camino que vuelv: Cycle: a path that returns to the starting point.
<strong>Conexo</strong>: se puede llegar: Connected: you can get from any vertex to any other.
<strong>Árbol</strong>: grafo conexo sin: Tree: a connected graph with no cycles. It always has exactly $V-1$ edges.
Se lee: <em>«el sumatorio, extendido a t:
Read as: “the sum, over all vertices v, of the degree of v, equals two times the number of edges”.

The reason is the one that gives it its name: each edge joins two vertices, so on adding up everyone's degrees, each edge is counted exactly twice. Just as at a gathering, if everyone counts how many hands they have shaken, the total is twice the number of handshakes there were.
Esa fórmula tiene una lectura graciosa:: That formula has an amusing reading: if at a party you count all the handshakes each person has given, the total is twice the number of handshakes, because two people take part in each. And from that comes a curious corollary: the number of people who have given an odd number of handshakes is always even.

La ciudad de Königsberg tenía siete puen: The city of Königsberg had seven bridges over the river Pregel. The townspeople wondered whether it was possible to take a walk crossing each bridge exactly once. In 1736, Euler proved that it was not, and in doing so founded graph theory and topology.
Su razonamiento fue este: en cada zona d: His reasoning was this: at each piece of land you pass through, you have to enter by one bridge and leave by another, so you need an even number of bridges. Only the starting point and the finishing point can have an odd number. In Königsberg all four areas had an odd number of bridges. Impossible.

El «sobre abierto» tiene cinco vértices:: The “open envelope” has five vertices: the four corners of a square (1, 2, 3, 4) and the flap tip (5). Its eight edges are the four sides, the two diagonals and the two sides of the flap, which joins 3 and 4. Can it be drawn without lifting the pencil or repeating a line?
<strong>Los grados.</strong> Esquinas de: The degrees. Bottom corners, 1 and 2: two sides and one diagonal each, degree 3. Top corners, 3 and 4: two sides, one diagonal and the flap side, degree 4. The tip, 5: degree 2.

El problema de los siete puentes se lo p: The seven bridges problem was a Sunday pastime for the people of Königsberg until Euler solved it in 1736 by proving that it had no solution. His contribution was deeper than the answer: he realised that the shape of the city, the distances and the size of the islands were irrelevant, and that all that mattered was what was connected to what. With that abstraction he founded two disciplines at once, graph theory and topology.
Un <strong>árbol</strong> es un grafo co: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles: the cheapest way of keeping everything connected. If you remove any edge, it splits in two; if you add any, a cycle appears.
Los árboles salen por todas partes en cu: Trees turn up everywhere as soon as you look, and one of the places they work hardest is inside programs. When a computer reads the formula $2 + 3 \cdot 4$, the first thing it does is turn it into a tree with the operations at the nodes and the numbers at the leaves; walking it from the bottom up is computing, and walking it writing instructions instead of results is compiling. It is in [[len-arbol|the block on machines and languages]], and it is a case where the structure is not a way of drawing the problem: it is the problem.
El <strong>árbol de expansión mínimo</st: The minimum spanning tree answers a very practical question: if $n$ cities have to be connected with optical fibre and each stretch has a cost, what is the cheapest network joining them all? Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms find it, and they are surprisingly simple: keep adding the cheapest edge that does not close a cycle.
El problema del <strong>camino mínimo</s: The shortest path problem (what is the shortest route from A to B?) is solved by Dijkstra's algorithm, from 1956. It is the one underneath any satnav and any route app you have used.
Los números son las distancias de cada t: The numbers are the distances of each stretch. Choose the destination and the shortest route from A is marked, with its total length.
De A a D hay un camino directo por B de: From A to D there is a direct route via B of length $4 + 5 = 9$ and another via C of $2 + 8 = 10$. Will either be the shortest, or is there a better one with more stretches?
El algoritmo de caminos mínimos es el qu: The shortest-path algorithm is the one your phone runs every time you ask for a route, with the streets as edges and the travel time as weight. The same algorithm routes internet packets hop by hop, decides the cheapest power line connecting a few villages and organises the order of the tasks on a building site. It is among the algorithms run most often per second on the planet.
Un árbol tiene un uso que parece menor y: A tree has one use that looks minor and holds up a good part of the internet: summarising a lot of data in a single number in such a way that one particular item can be proved to be inside without showing the rest. It is the Merkle tree, with a digest at each leaf and the blend of the two children at each node, and it is in [[cr-cadena|blockchains and Merkle trees]]. The check costs the logarithm of the number of leaves, which is the height of the tree.
Dos problemas parecidos y muy distintos: Two similar and very different problems
Un <strong>circuito euleriano</strong> p: An Eulerian circuit passes once through each edge; a Hamiltonian circuit passes once through each vertex. They sound almost the same, and yet:
Decidir si existe un circuito <strong>eu: Deciding whether an Eulerian circuit exists is trivial: you look at the degrees and that is that.
Decidir si existe uno <strong>hamiltonia: Deciding whether a Hamiltonian one exists is among the hardest problems known (NP-complete): nobody knows how to do it quickly for large graphs.
El problema del <em>viajante de comercio: The travelling salesman problem (visiting $n$ cities by the shortest route) is the weighted version of the Hamiltonian circuit. With 20 cities there are more than $10^{17}$ possible routes. If anyone found a fast algorithm, they would incidentally solve the P vs NP problem, one of the seven Millennium Problems, with a prize of a million dollars.

Dos dibujos muy distintos pueden ser el: Two very different drawings can be the same graph, and one with crossing lines can be planar. Only the vertices and who joins whom count.

«La ruta más corta es la de menos tramos: “The shortest route is the one with fewest stretches”
De A a D, dos tramos suman 9 y tres tram: From A to D, two stretches add up to 9 and three stretches add up to 8. What is minimised is the total length, not the number of stops.
Euleriano recorre todas las <em>aristas<: Eulerian covers all the edges; Hamiltonian, all the vertices. The first is settled by counting degrees; the second is among the hardest problems there are.
Que un problema tenga solución eficiente: That one problem has an efficient solution and its twin does not is the heart of the most important open question in computer science, P versus NP, with a million-dollar prize waiting. It is not philosophy: if anyone proved they are equal, all present-day cryptography would fall in a weekend. Meanwhile, delivery firms and factories solve their routes with methods that give a good solution without guaranteeing it is the best.
